> This document answers one question about our Group B project: **not "what
> did we do?", but "why did we do it that way?"** For every check in the QC
> report (`01-qc.html`) and every step in the three analyses
> (`dataset-overview.html`), it explains why we chose that method, why we
> drew the figure that way, why we picked that filter or threshold — and, in
> every case, an alternative we did *not* choose.
>
> It is a companion page, not a new analysis: no new numbers are computed
> here. Every number quoted already appears in the QC report or the main
> overview, and you can verify each one with the check-yourself commands
> those pages give.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

# How to read this page

Each entry has the same shape:

- **What we did** — one line, in plain words.
- **Why this method** — the reasoning, including why the problem made this
  the natural tool.
- **Why we represented it that way** — why the figure/table looks how it
  looks (log scale, colour choice, bar chart vs scatter, and so on).
- **Not chosen** — a real alternative we passed on, and why.

A few terms that come up repeatedly, defined once here:

- **Compositional data**: sequencing gives each sample a fixed number of
  reads, so everything is a *share* of the total. If one species goes up,
  others must look like they went down. Absolute amount and relative share
  are different claims.
- **Normalisation**: putting samples with different sequencing depths on the
  same footing before testing.
- **Adjusted p-value**: a p-value corrected for the fact that we ran
  thousands of tests at once; without the correction, 5% of them would pass
  by luck.

---

# Part 1 — the QC report (`01-qc.html`)

The QC report exists because a mistake at the top of a pipeline contaminates
everything below it. We checked the boring-but-fatal things *first*: sample
alignment, missing values, sequencing depth, sparsity, batch effects. Each
section explains what could go wrong if we skipped it.

## 1.1 Checking the sample sheet first

**What we did.** Looked at the metadata: 93 unique sample IDs, no missing
cells, and the shape of the three arms (28 pill / 39 injectable / 26 ring).

**Why this method.** The sample sheet is the *row of truth* — every other
table gets matched to it. If it has duplicate IDs or gaps, every later join
silently mismatches samples. We also counted the arms because unequal group
sizes matter for statistical power later: with 26 ring users against 39
injectable, comparisons involving the ring arm are the noisiest, and no test
can fix that. Either way, we needed to know the shape before choosing tests.

**Why we represented it that way.** The BV-by-arm chart uses
`position = "fill"` (stacked proportions, not counts) because the arms are
unequal — with raw counts, a bigger arm automatically looks like it has more
BV, which would be meaningless. Proportions make the arms directly
comparable.

**Not chosen.** Reading the CSV by eye in a spreadsheet — it cannot detect
duplicate IDs or tell you which tables share the same sample order.

## 1.2 Checking that all tables describe the same 93 samples

**What we did.** Compared the column order of both count tables (and the
cytokine table) against the metadata row order, with `identical()`.

**Why this method.** DESeq2 matches count-matrix columns to the design table
by **position, not by name** — it will not warn if they disagree, it will
just produce wrong results. Our `read_counts()` helper already reorders the
columns to match the metadata, but we check anyway: the check costs one line
and the failure mode is silent. The workshop rule "check the order" exists
for exactly this reason.

**Why we represented it that way.** There is deliberately no figure — this
is a yes/no check. A single `FALSE` should stop everything until fixed, so
a number that is easy to spot (a bare `TRUE` line) is the right presentation.

**Not chosen.** Trusting the loader without verifying, or eyeballing a few
sample IDs. Silent misalignment is the single most dangerous failure in this
kind of analysis, and neither alternative would reliably catch it.

## 1.3 Sequencing depth (library size)

**What we did.** Computed total reads per sample for both tables, drew three
views — a histogram, a sorted bar chart with an alarm line at 10% of the
median, and a scatter of species-depth against gene-depth — and named the
five shallowest samples.

**Why this method.** A sample sequenced far less than the others detects
fewer things *because it was sequenced less*, not because its biology
differs. Before any test we need to know whether any sample sits far below
the rest. We found one: **B006** (5,247 species reads vs a median near
29,000 — roughly a sixth of the median).

**Why we represented it that way.** Each of the three views answers a
different question, and one figure could not answer all three:

- the **histogram** shows the shape of the whole distribution (one broad lump
  = healthy);
- the **sorted bar chart** makes the one outlier easy to *name* — a histogram
  can show a lump displaced to the left but cannot tell you which sample;
- the **scatter** (species depth vs gene depth) distinguishes two very
  different problems: if B006 were shallow in *both* tables, the library
  itself failed; since B006 is fine for genes, the problem is a low-yield
  bacterial extraction, not a broken sample.

The red line sits at **10% of the median** because we wanted a simple,
defensible alarm bell. Log scale on the histogram because library sizes span
an order of magnitude — on a linear scale the outlier would squash every
other bar into invisibility.

**Not chosen.** A fixed 1,000-read floor (arbitrary — why 1,000?) or
interquartile-range outlier rules (more formal, but easier to defend to a
biologist as "a sixth of a typical sample"). We also did **not drop B006
here**: dropping is a per-analysis decision that belongs in each analysis
report, where its effect on the results can be seen.

## 1.4 Sparsity and dominance

**What we did.** Measured the fraction of zeros in each table, the largest
share any single feature holds in a sample, species prevalence (in how many
samples is each species seen?), and a rank-abundance curve for one
median-depth sample.

**Why this method.** Both tables are compositional, and composition dictates
which methods are legal later. The species table is ~88% zeros and one
*Lactobacillus* often exceeds half the reads — that sparsity is exactly why
we chose composition-aware methods (DESeq2's negative-binomial model, CLR
thinking) for the species table. The gene table is dense (~3% zeros), so it
can take the standard RNA-seq pipeline unchanged. Deciding this *before*
analysis avoids retrofitting methods.

**Why we represented it that way.** The **prevalence histogram** shows the
classic microbiome shape — most species detected in only a handful of
samples, a few in nearly all — which is what motivates the prevalence filter
used later. The **rank-abundance curve** shows dominance in one picture: a
steep fall = one species dominates. We drew it for the *median-depth* sample
rather than the average or the best sample, because a median sample is the
most typical, and a single representative curve is easier to read than a
colour-by-arm grid of 93 curves.

**Not chosen.** Shannon diversity as the sparsity summary — it is a
different question (diversity within samples, which the main analysis tests
properly in its step 1). We also deferred the prevalence *filter* decision to
the analysis reports, where its effect on results is visible.

## 1.5 Are these really counts?

**What we did.** `stopifnot()` checks that both count tables are whole,
non-negative, and contain no missing values; then looked at where the
cytokines *do* have gaps.

**Why this method.** DESeq2 refuses (or misbehaves on) fractional or
negative values. This is a pass/fail gate, and the honest response to a
failure is to go back to the exporter — never to patch numbers by hand. It
is free insurance at this stage. The cytokines found two participants,
**B018 and B029**, missing *every* cytokine value — a whole-assay failure,
not scattered gaps.

**Why we represented it that way.** Again, no figure: a gate check should be
a statement, not a picture. The consequence, though, *is* worth stating in
every later report: cytokine analyses run on 91 samples, count-table
analyses on all 93, so results from the two arms of the project rest on
slightly different sample sets.

**Not chosen.** Silent assumptions ("the data came from a pipeline, it must
be fine") — the workshop rule is that DESeq2 will not warn you.

## 1.6 Feature annotations

**What we did.** Checked every counted taxon and gene has exactly one
annotation row, and looked at what kinds of genes are in the annotation.

**Why this method.** A feature we can count but not name is one we cannot
interpret or report. Full coverage in both tables passed. One real catch:
**two different Ensembl genes share a symbol**, so any analysis that
aggregates per symbol (including microViz's `tax_transform(rank = "symbol")`)
would silently merge two distinct genes' counts.

**Why we represented it that way.** The annotation-category bar chart uses a
**log-scaled y-axis** because a few categories have thousands of genes and
most have dozens — a linear axis would render the small bars unreadable.

**Not chosen.** Aggregating by gene symbol anyway — rejected because of the
duplicate-symbol catch; we aggregate per Ensembl gene ID instead.

## 1.7 Cytokines

**What we did.** Looked at the range of each cytokine, plotted all 15 on one
log-scale boxplot, and tabulated each cytokine's minimum value.

**Why this method.** Cytokines are concentrations (pg/mL), not counts, and
they are measured with a **lower limit of detection (LLOD)** — the smallest
amount the assay can reliably distinguish from zero. Several cytokines have
minimum values that repeat *suspiciously exactly* (e.g. 0.005 pg/mL): those
are the LLOD floor, not true measurements. Knowing this before modelling
prevents treating 0.005 as a real number.

**Why we represented it that way.** The boxplot is on a **log scale and
flipped horizontal** — cytokines vary over orders of magnitude, so only log
scale is honest, and 15 labelled cytokines read far better as horizontal
boxes. The flat line of crammed points at the bottom of each box *is* the
LLOD story, visible at a glance. The minimum-value chart makes the repeated
floor values directly comparable across cytokines.

**Not chosen.** Correcting sub-LLOD values here (e.g. imputation or
substitution) — that decision belongs to whichever report actually models
cytokines, because the right handling depends on the model.

## 1.8 Batch effects

**What we did.** Cross-tabulated the two RNA-seq batches (B1, B2) against
the three arms, and compared gene library sizes between batches (boxplot and
overlaid density curves).

**Why this method.** Batch effects are systematic differences between
processing runs that can masquerade as biology. They are only *dangerous*,
though, when tangled with the grouping variable — if every pill sample were
in batch B1 and every ring sample in B2, "arm" and "batch" would be
indistinguishable. The cross-tabulation tests exactly that: both batches
contain all three arms in similar numbers (pill 14/14, injectable 20/19,
ring 13/13), so batch and arm are **not confounded**.

**Why we represented it that way.** The boxplot is a crude check for a level
shift between batches; the **overlaid density curves** are the stricter
check — if the two curves sit on top of each other (they nearly do), the
batches are interchangeable. Both are shown because a boxplot hides shape
differences that densities reveal.

**Not chosen.** An ordination coloured by batch at QC stage — deferred to
the analyses, which keep `rnaseq_batch` as a covariate in every DE model
anyway (standard practice even when the QC looks clean).

## 1.9 The verdict table

**What we did.** Summarised every check as pass / issue / action, with the
one real decision highlighted (what to do with B006 in species work).

**Why this method.** A QC report that does not end in a list of decisions is
just a notebook. The table format forces each check to have a stated
consequence, and highlights that nothing blocks the analysis.

**Why we represented it that way.** The report also ends with
**check-yourself commands** (e.g. `colSums(spec)[order(colSums(spec))[1:5]]`
should print B006 at 5,247) — because every claim in QC should be
independently verifiable with one line of code, in case we made an error
writing the report itself.

# Part 2 — Question 1: does the microbiome differ by contraceptive arm?

*(Numbers and figures from `analysis-microbiome-arm.R`, reported in
`dataset-overview.html`.)*

## Step 0 — Are the arms comparable to begin with?

**What we did.** Compared library sizes across arms before any test.

**Why this method.** If one arm had been sequenced much more deeply, any
later difference could be a depth difference. This is the same check as in
the QC report, now *stratified by arm* — QC looked at samples one at a
time; here we look at groups.

**Why we represented it that way.** A single faceted bar chart (fig1) with
all three arms side by side — the question is comparative, so the picture
should be too.

## Step 1 — Alpha diversity (diversity *within* a sample)

**What we did.** Computed Shannon diversity per sample, compared arms with a
Kruskal–Wallis test plus pairwise Wilcoxon tests, and drew boxplots (fig2).

**Why Shannon.** Shannon captures *both* how many species are present
(richness) and how evenly their reads are spread (evenness). The main
alternative, observed species count, sees only richness and would miss a
sample shifting from Lactobacillus-dominance towards an even mix.

**Why Kruskal–Wallis rather than ANOVA.** Shannon values here are not
normally distributed and the groups are modest in size; a rank-based test
makes no distributional assumption. Pairwise Wilcoxon tests follow it up
because the overall test only says "somewhere differs", not which pair.

**Why we represented it that way.** Boxplots (not bar charts of means)
because they show the full spread — and the *overlapping* boxes are the
honest picture: pill's median (0.90) sits below injectable's (1.74), but the
overlap is heavy, which is exactly what the non-significant p = 0.47 says. A
bar chart of means would have hidden that nuance.

**Not chosen.** ANOVA on log-transformed values — works, but assumes
normality of the transformed values and buys nothing here.

## Step 2 — What the communities are made of

**What we did.** Stacked-bar composition plots (fig3) coloured by phylum.

**Why this method.** Before testing *whether* communities differ, look at
*what* they are made of — it grounds every later result in biology (here:
Lactobacillus-dominated vs anaerobe-rich samples).

**Why we represented it that way.** Stacked bars are the standard grammar
for compositional data, but they must be read as *shares*, not amounts —
the compositional caveat. Colouring by phylum (not species) keeps the
picture legible at 93 samples.

## Step 3 — Beta diversity: does the *whole community* differ?

**What we did.** Computed Bray–Curtis distances between all pairs of
samples, ordinated them with PCoA (fig4), and tested group separation with
PERMANOVA (`adonis2`) at 999 permutations — a full model
(`arm + bv + any_sti + batch`) and arm alone.

**Why Bray–Curtis.** It is the standard ecological distance for
community-composition data and is interpretable ("these two samples share
about x% of their community"). We discussed the Aitchison distance on
CLR-transformed counts — arguably more correct for compositional data — but
chose Bray–Curtis for interpretability, and because the sparsity is
moderate.

**Why PCoA.** It gives exact axis-variance percentages (fig4's axis labels),
which is what lets us say the three arms intermingle. NMDS would order
samples but not give those percentages.

**Why PERMANOVA at 999 permutations.** Distances between samples are not
independent (every sample appears in many pairs), so ordinary ANOVA on
coordinates would be invalid. PERMANOVA is the standard fix, and 999
permutations gives p-values stable enough to report. The **full model**
adjusts for BV, STI and batch, because the QC showed BV dominates this
dataset — testing arm *without* it would mostly re-discover BV. The
**arm-alone** model is reported alongside so the reader can see how weak the
raw association is (R² ≈ 0.03, p ≈ 0.1).

**Why we represented it that way.** The PCoA is coloured by arm so that the
permutation result can be checked visually: three intermingling colours
*should* accompany a small R². If the test said "significant" while the
plot showed clean separation by accident of colouring, one of them would be
wrong.

**Not chosen.** PERMANOVA adjusted only for batch — it answers a different
question and would give BV credit for arm differences.

## Step 4 — Which species differ? (DESeq2)

**What we did.** DESeq2 on raw species counts, design
`~ rnaseq_batch + bv + arm`, minimal filter, Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted
p < 0.05, results as a top-hits bar chart (fig5) and tables.

**Why raw counts.** The workshop's central rule: DESeq2 does its own
normalisation internally (size factors) and expects the unnormalised,
unlogged counts it was designed for. CPM or logged values would invalidate
its dispersion model. We report this here because it is the single easiest
rule to break.

**Why this design.** Three covariates, each with a reason:

- `rnaseq_batch` — QC showed two batches; even unconfounded, adjusting
  removes residual noise.
- `bv` — BV *is* the species table in summary form; leaving it out would
  attribute BV-driven differences to the arm.
- No `any_sti` — a defensible choice at the time; the methods review
  (`02-methods-review.html`) later recommended adding it for consistency
  with the PERMANOVA model. We note the inconsistency rather than pretend
  it does not exist.

**Why that filter.** Total reads ≥ 10 per species, keeping 110 of 220
species. The purpose is to reduce noise and the multiple-testing burden.
It is deliberately *minimal* — a stricter filter changes results, and we
wanted the most standard, most reproducible choice. (The review also notes
a prevalence-based filter, presence in ≥ 5 samples, would keep 72 species
and shrink the testing burden further — worth considering next time.)

**Why adjusted p < 0.05 (Benjamini–Hochberg).** With 220 species tested at
once, unadjusted p-values would guarantee false positives (5% of 220 ≈ 11
species "significant" by luck). BH controls the false-discovery rate — the
fraction of significant results expected to be false — which is the standard
correction for many simultaneous tests. p < 0.1 would be more sensitive at
the cost of more false positives; we stayed with the conventional 0.05.

**Why we represented it that way.** The bar chart (fig5) shows the largest
log2 fold changes among significant species — the size of each difference,
signed by direction. One honest caveat, flagged in the overview and made
concrete by the review: raw log2FCs from low-count species (e.g.
*Atopobium minutum*, +28.3 on an average of 18 reads) are unreliable, and
shrinking them (`lfcShrink`) reorders the chart substantially. The
*significance* lists are unaffected.

**Not chosen.** Defining groups from the counts themselves — violates the
workshop rule (never define a group from a table and test that same table);
groups come from the metadata (`arm`), the table is only tested.

## Question 1 — why this overall shape?

Four steps, in order of *coarseness*: depth → diversity → whole community →
individual species. Each step's result conditions how to read the next:
weak differences at step 3 mean the species list at step 4 is a short,
consistent story (BV-associated anaerobes in ring/injectable users), not a
genomic upheaval. Presenting them in this order makes the modest conclusion
unavoidable rather than buried.

# Part 3 — Question 2: does the ring differ from the systemic methods in host gene expression?

## The grouping decision: `route` (local vs systemic)

**What we did.** Collapsed pill + injectable into one "systemic" group and
tested ring (local) against it.

**Why this method.** The ring delivers hormone *at the vagina*; pill and
injectable deliver it through the bloodstream. If the local-vs-systemic
route is the biologically meaningful distinction, testing it directly has
more power than three pairwise arm contrasts — one comparison instead of
two, on groups of 26 vs 67. The group is defined from the **metadata**
(`arm`), never from the gene table — the workshop rule, kept precisely.

**Why we represented it that way.** The route table (26 ring, 67 systemic)
is printed in full so the collapse is visible and checkable.

**Not chosen.** Testing the three arms separately and arguing from the
pattern — less direct, and the pairing of comparisons would need its own
multiplicity correction.

## Step 0 — comparable sequencing depth

Same reasoning as QC section 1.3, now per group: gene depths (5.9–24
million reads) are comfortably even, so no sample needs excluding from the
gene analysis.

## Step 1 — the big picture: PCA (fig7)

**What we did.** PCA on variance-stabilised (VST) values of the 500 most
variable genes, coloured by route.

**Why VST.** Raw RNA-seq counts have variance that grows with the mean,
which would let a handful of highly expressed genes dominate every axis.
VST makes variance roughly constant across the expression range — the
standard transform for *visualising* expression data.

**Why VST here but never for the test.** This is the workshop's second rule
stated again: transforms are for pictures, DESeq2's model is for raw
counts. Keeping the two strictly separate is what makes every downstream
p-value defensible.

**Why the top 500 most variable genes.** PCA on all 14,226 genes is
dominated by thousands of unchanging, low-expression genes that add noise,
not signal. Ranking by variance selects the genes that carry the structure
the plot is meant to show. 500 rather than 2,000 because this is a
visualisation, not a test — enough genes for a stable picture, few enough
to stay dominated by real structure.

**Why we represented it that way.** PCA (not UMAP or t-SNE) because PCA
axes are linear and their loadings are interpretable — you can ask *which
genes* pull a sample to the right, which is exactly how fig8's genes were
found.

## Step 2 — the formal test: DESeq2 on raw gene counts

**What we did.** DESeq2 with design `~ rnaseq_batch + bv + any_sti + route`,
raw counts, adjusted p < 0.05.

**Why DESeq2 rather than limma-voom.** DESeq2 was already the workshop
tool, is designed for raw counts exactly like ours, and its dispersion
model suits small samples. Either method is defensible; switching tools
mid-project would add re-learning, not accuracy.

**Why these covariates.** Same logic as Question 1 plus one:

- `rnaseq_batch` — QC-checked, kept as insurance.
- `bv` — the ring arm had the most BV-like microbiome; without adjusting,
  BV-driven host responses would be attributed to the ring.
- `any_sti` — STI inflammation could mimic a route effect, so it is held
  constant. Entered as 0/1 numeric (a factor is equivalent for two levels).

**Why that filter.** Total reads ≥ 10 per gene — minimal, for the same
reasons as Question 1. The review later showed this particular filter keeps
*all* 14,226 genes (a no-op, since no gene is that rare) — we report that
honestly rather than pretend it trimmed anything.

**Why adjusted p < 0.05.** With 14,226 tests, the multiple-testing problem
is far bigger than in Question 1; BH correction is not optional here.

**Why we represented it that way.** The bar chart (fig8) is signed by
direction (orange = higher in ring, blue = higher in systemic) so the two
gene *programmes* — secretory/inflammatory vs squamous-epithelial — are
visible as a pattern, not just a list. The tables rank by adjusted p-value
rather than fold change, deliberately: p-value order is more stable than
raw log2FC order, which is exactly the lesson from fig5.

**Not chosen.** Testing on CPM or logged values — violates the raw-counts
rule. Requiring a minimum log2FC in addition to padj < 0.05 — defensible,
but it hides low-fold-change genes that are nonetheless very well supported;
we preferred listing effect sizes so readers can apply their own judgement.

## Step 3 — the consistency check

**What we did.** Fitted a separate model with `arm` in the design and
compared ring-vs-pill (60 significant genes) and ring-vs-injectable (87)
contrasts: 11 genes significant in both, all pointing the same direction.

**Why this method.** If "local vs systemic" is the real story, ring should
differ from *both* systemic methods in the *same* direction. Agreement
between two independently fitted models is evidence the signal is about the
route, not about one particular pair. The review later suggested a cleaner
one-number version: contrast pill directly against injectable (only 4
significant genes) — showing the two systemic arms are nearly
interchangeable. Both versions support the collapse; the direct contrast is
the one to lead with next time.

**Why we represented it that way.** A three-row table (60 / 87 / 11-shared,
same direction) rather than a Venn diagram — the numbers are few, and the
*direction* agreement is the point.

## Question 2 — overall answer and why it is phrased so carefully

**Why "yes, modestly but consistently".** 66 of 14,226 genes (0.5%) is
small; the *coherence* of the two gene programmes and the agreement between
the two contrasts is what makes the finding believable. The BPIFA1 caution —
it is bacteria-induced, and the ring arm is the most BV-like — is stated in
the overview because the cross-sectional design cannot separate "the ring
affected the tissue" from "the ring shifted the microbiome, and the tissue
responded". Adjusting for BV helps but cannot fully untangle a mediator.

# Part 4 — Question 3: community type vs method — which explains host genes better?

## Step 1 — defining community types from the *microbiome*

**What we did.** Bray–Curtis distances between participants' microbiomes,
Ward's clustering, cut into k = 3 groups (chosen by best mean silhouette
among k = 2–5), named by dominant species (crispatus-dominant /
iners-dominant / diverse).

**Why cluster at all.** Contraceptive *arm* is a label; microbiome
*community type* is a pattern discovered in the data. Clustering asks
whether participants fall into natural microbiome states — the classic
community state types — without assuming the arm labels matter.

**Why Bray–Curtis + Ward.** Bray–Curtis for the same reasons as Question 1's
beta diversity (standard, interpretable). Ward's method minimises within-
cluster variance and produces compact, evenly sized clusters, which suits
comparison of groups later.

**Why k = 3.** Chosen by **mean silhouette** — a measure of how well each
sample sits in its cluster — across k = 2–5 (best: 0.323 at k = 3). This is
a data-driven choice with a stated criterion, rather than an arbitrary
pick. The planned robustness check (rerun with k = 2 and see whether
conclusions survive) is the right follow-up, and is suggested in the
overview's check-yourself section.

**Why we named clusters by biology.** "C1–C3" forces the reader to memorise
a code; "crispatus-dominant / iners-dominant / diverse" carries the biology
in the name. Naming by dominant species is verifiable (fig10 shows the
composition of each type).

**Why this respects the one-table rule.** The types are defined **from the
species table** and tested **against the gene table** — the group is never
defined and tested on the same table. This is the workshop rule the whole
question is built to demonstrate.

## Step 2 — testing which grouping explains genes better

**What we did.** Two complementary comparisons, because "explains more" can
mean two different things:

1. **Per-gene**: DESeq2 likelihood-ratio tests (LRT) with design
   `~ rnaseq_batch + bv + any_sti + grouping`, once with `ctype_lab`, once
   with `arm` — counting significant genes for each (93 vs 49).
2. **Genome-wide**: PERMANOVA on VST values of the 2,000 most variable
   genes, Euclidean distances — R² for each grouping (0.020 vs 0.032).

**Why the LRT rather than pairwise Wald tests.** Community type has three
levels; a Wald test would need all pairwise contrasts unioned, with messy
multiplicity logic. The LRT handles a multi-level grouping in one test per
gene: "does this grouping improve the model's fit at all?"

**Why adjust for BV in both models.** The diverse type is 37/39 BV-positive
— nearly a synonym for BV. Without the BV covariate, the comparison would
mostly re-discover BV rather than ask the intended question. This is a
choice we state explicitly because it *narrows* the claim: "type beyond
what BV already explains".

**Why PERMANOVA on VST top-2,000 with Euclidean distance.** For gene
expression, the natural distance is Euclidean on a variance-stabilised
scale — the same VST rationale as fig7, applied to more genes because this
is a test of overall structure, not a picture. Using all genes or raw
counts would be noisier for the same reason as before.

**Why report two views rather than one.** A single "which explains more"
number would force a false choice: counting significant genes asks about
*individual genes*; R² asks about the *whole expression profile*. The split
verdict (type wins on gene counts; method edges it genome-wide, though
neither R² is clearly significant) *is* the finding — forcing one story
would have discarded the more interesting answer.

**Why the caveat that the two comparisons are not a formal test of each
other.** Counting significant genes from separate models is a heuristic;
the two numbers come from different tests and cannot be compared with a
p-value as they stand. The overview says so plainly. (The review's nested
LRTs — 162 vs 70 genes — make the comparison properly formal and reach the
same conclusion; adopting that approach is the main recommended upgrade.)

**Not chosen.** A single formal non-nested model comparison — not standard
for DESeq2 grouping variables and harder to explain; the two-view framing
is the simpler honest choice.

# Part 5 — cross-cutting decisions

These apply everywhere, so they are collected here rather than repeated.

| Decision | Why | Not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| Groups defined from metadata only (`arm`, `route`) | Never define a group from a count table and test that same table — circular reasoning guarantees "findings" | Defining `route` or community types from the gene table |
| Raw counts into DESeq2; VST only for figures | DESeq2's normalisation and dispersion model assume raw counts | CPM, log2, or TPM inputs |
| Column order checked before every test (`stopifnot`) | DESeq2 matches by position and will not warn otherwise | Trusting the loader |
| Adjusted p < 0.05 (Benjamini–Hochberg) | Standard FDR control for thousands of simultaneous tests; stricter cutoffs hide well-supported results, looser ones inflate false positives | Unadjusted p-values; p < 0.1 |
| Covariate adjustment (`batch`, `bv`, and `any_sti` where relevant) | QC showed batch balance and BV dominance; adjustment removes known alternative explanations | Unadjusted models as the only model (review recommends reporting both — adopted as the change to make) |
| Minimal count filters (≥ 10 total reads) | Reduce noise with the smallest possible assumption; stricter filters change results and would need their own justification | No filter (slower, noisier); aggressive prevalence filters (worth a follow-up — see the review) |
| No samples dropped | QC found nothing requiring exclusion; B006 matters only for the species table and was handled there | Dropping the 3 intermediate-BV samples (kept: BV is a covariate, not a grouping variable) |
| Every number paired with a check-yourself command | A report the reader can falsify is worth more than one they must trust | Report-only pages |
| Compositional caveats stated wherever a relative-abundance claim is made | "The share of X went down" ≠ "there was less X" — sequencing depth is fixed per sample | Ignoring compositionality |

---

## Choices made

*(For this document itself, per the workshop convention.)*

- Explained the QC report section by section and the three questions step by
  step, mirroring the order of the original documents — alternative: a
  single alphabetical list of decisions (harder to follow while reading the
  original reports side by side).
- Quoted only numbers already published in `01-qc.html` and
  `dataset-overview.html`; no new computation — alternative: recomputing
  everything here (duplicates the scripts and risks the two pages drifting).
- Used tables for the cross-cutting decisions and bullet blocks for each
  step — alternative: all prose (harder to scan) or all tables (no room for
  the reasoning).
- Included the methods review's corrections (shrinkage, no-op filter,
  nested LRTs) as noted follow-ups rather than rewriting the analyses to
  match — alternative: silently describing the *corrected* analyses, which
  would make this page disagree with the reports it explains.
- Plain default Quarto styling — alternative: copying the overview's custom
  CSS (cosmetic; not worth the extra file).

*To check this page against the originals:* open `01-qc.html` and
`dataset-overview.html` beside it; every claim here has a one-line source in
those documents, and their check-yourself commands verify the underlying
numbers.
